title: 2026 Home Run Derby bats, winner’s chain and special autographed balls explained
content:
The art, history and food of Philadelphia are consistent themes throughout the 2026 MLB All-Star festivities, and that holds true for much of the equipment created for the Home Run Derby. Here’s what you need to know about the bats, the winner’s chain and the special baseballs being used in the event.

Victus made two Philly-centric bats for Bryce Harper. One represents the slabs of meat that Rocky Balboa famously used for heavy-bag training in Rocky. The other bat sticks with the boxing theme, this time incorporating Harper’s pal, the Phillie Phanatic. Pushing the Phanatic as a boxer with a black eye, Apollo Creed-esque shorts, a Liberty Bell chain around his neck, and the word “Jawn” in the style of the city’s Love statue.

Harper also received bats from Marucci. One features “Harper: King of Steaks” (a reference to Philadelphia landmark cheesesteak restaurant Pat’s) written beneath a depiction of the Phillies’ first baseman dressed in Revolutionary War garb and chowing down on a sandwich. Another is illustrated with a bald eagle and the Liberty Bell, while a third, commemorative All-Star Game bat is decorated in red, gold and blue, with stars on the handle along with Harper’s name and the date of the game on the barrel.

Jordan Walker’s lumber from Victus introduces the world to “Walker Industries” with an Iron Man theme. Munetaka Murakami has a Victus bat emblazoned with a fire-breathing dragon (although he used a standard game bat during the first round of the Home Run Derby).

Willson Contreras has a Bowser bat, a reference to the nickname his teammates gave him back in his St. Louis Cardinals days.

Junior Caminero’s bat depicts his lucky No. 13 on a blinged-out chain (but he also used a normal game bat instead), and Jac Caglianone’s is centered around his Christian faith, with a crown of thorns and a John 3:16 reference.

Ben Rice’s Louisville Slugger represents New York City with an image of the skyline, the Statue of Liberty and the New York Yankees’ first baseman’s name written in graffiti-style letters, while Kyle Schwarber’s incorporates the Philadelphia skyline and his jersey number.

Similar to previous years, each player participating in the derby has signed one to two dozen balls that will be dumped into the basket of balls to be used in the competition. The signed balls will be mixed with unsigned ones, which means there’s no guarantee that the balls thrown to the batters will be the special autographed ones. What happens if one is hit but it doesn’t reach the stands? Anyone shagging balls in the outfield has to return them. The plan for what happens to any autographed balls that don’t end up with fans during the derby is still to be determined, according to MLB.

MLB dreamed up the winner’s chain as a complement to the existing Home Run Derby trophy in 2019.

John Luongo, now creative director of social design for MLB, then a designer with the league’s social media team, got involved in 2022 from his interest in fashion and his prior work as a designer. That’s when he found New York jewelry designer Kenny Hwang. When MLB decided to create the winner’s chain, Luongo said, “It was very close (to the derby), so we needed a talented and trustworthy designer and jeweler who could work quickly and skillfully. Kenny had prior relationships with our colleagues and expressed interest, with a knack for moving quickly.”

For the 2026 Home Run Derby, Hwang designed a Liberty Bell chain, complete with a functional clapper that makes the bell ring and swing. It features a lining of rubies and sapphires, with text on the lower banner that reads “Ring the Bell” in a clear nod to the Phillies’ home run celebration at Citizens Bank Park. In this detail, 250 custom-cut rubies signify America’s 250th anniversary, arranged in a pattern that’s meant to resemble Philadelphia’s cobblestone streets. In total, the chain has 41 carats of diamonds, 41 carats of rubies, and 10 carats of sapphires.

The 2024 and 2025 chains are currently in the American Museum of Natural History in New York as part of an “Objects of Sports Excellence” exhibit, but each chain is normally kept by the winner of the annual event.
